full_judgment:
2. The facts, relevant for disposal of this petition, are that the petitioners as pre-emptors instituted the original Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No.40 of 2004 under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 in the 1st Court of the Joint District Judge, Cumilla for getting an order of preemption of 113/4 decimals land transferred on 18.11.2002 by a sale deed stating that 37 decimals land appertaining to Plot No. 1824 corresponding to B.S. Plot No. 4106 of R.S. Khatian No.600 under Mouza-Kandirpar of Police Station-Kotwali, District-Cumilla originally belonged to one Sushila Sundori Pal who died intestate leaving behind her legal heirs three sons, namely, Priyalal Pal, Chuni Lal Pal and Manindra Kishore Pal. At the demise of Manindra Kishore Pal, his share devolved upon his two sons, namely, Tarun Kanti Pal and Jhantu Pal. Priyalal Pal, Chuni Lal Pal and Tarun Kanti Pal transferred 37 decimals land in favour of one Mohini Mohan Dastidar by a sub-kabala dated 15.01.1974 which was subsequently gifted by Mohini Mohon to his three sons, namely, Dolon Ghosh Dastidar, Raton Ghosh Dastidar and Sadhan Ghosh Dastidar on 31.07.1985. Thereafter, Dolon Ghosh Dastidar transferred his 11 decimals land in favour of one Bhupesh Chandra Datta by a sale deed dated 28.01.1986. Sadhan Ghosh Dastidar sold out his 03 decimals land corresponding to Plot No.1824 in favour of one Sheuli Chakraborty by a sale deed dated 23.01.1986 who sold that land in favour of Kabir Ahmed Chowdhury (Pre-emptor No.1) on 24.07.1993. Ratan Ghosh Dastidar and two others transferred 04 decimals land in favour of one Shyamal Chandra by a kabala deed dated 01.02.1986 who transferred some land in favour of Md. Yousuf Chowdhury Babul (Pre-emptor No.2) by a sale deed dated 09.03.1986 and 04 decimals land by another sale deed of the same date. Bhupesh Chandra Datta, thereafter, transferred the case land in favour of pre-emptee-respondent No.1 by the case kabala dated 18.11.2002. No notice was ever served upon the co-sharers and the pre-emptor-petitioners as co-sharers in the case holding. The further case of the pre-emptor-petitioners is that the purchaser (respondent No.1) is the stranger to the jute and knowing about the case kabala after obtaining certified copy of the trans-fer deed on 02.09.2004, the pre-emptor-petitioners filed the original case for get-ting the land pre-empted. 

 6. Mr. A. M. Aminuddin, Senior Advocate, appearing for the petitioners, submits that the High Court Division failed to appreciate the provisions of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural. Tenancy Act, 1949 in its true sense and thus wrongly held that the pre-emptors had no locus standi to seek preemption of the case holding. He further submits that the findings of the High Court Division to the effect that the pre-emptors ceased to be a co-sharer in the case land due to separation of case jote by way of mutation Khatian is not in accordance with law because of the fact that in a case of preemption if filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and if a co-sharer tenant owns a portion of land in any plot, he is to be a co-sharer in the entire plot even if the land of that plot is recorded in more than one khatians and as such, the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be interfered with by this Division. He further submits that the High Court Division has committed error of law in disallowing the appeal and dismissing the case without following the provisions of Order XXXIX, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 7. Mr. Probir Neogi, Senior Advocate, appearing for respondent No.1, supported the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. Mr. Neogi further contended that the trial Court was quite justified in holding the view that the pre-emptors are not the co-sharers in the case land and they have no right of preemption since by way of the separation of joma through mutation their co-sharership in the case holding has been ceased prior to filing of their case and thus they have no locus standi to file the original miscellaneous case for getting the case land pre-empted under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. He further contended that both the pre-emptors have mutated their land and separated the joma pursuant to their earlier purchase and opened a separate khatian and are paying rent to the Government separately and thereby in respect of the case land, they are not entitled to preempt the land by virtue of their cosharership in the case holding. He adds that in the year 1989 and 1.993 respectively, pre-emptor No.1 and his predecessor-in-interest got their names mutated vide Mutation Case Nos.471/1988-89 and 92/1993-94 and pre-emptor No.2 has also got his name mutated pursuant to Mutation Case No.563/1988-89 and besides this, the predecessor-in-interest of the pre-emptee-respondent, namely, Bhupesh Chandra Datta also got his name mutated in respect of the case land by virtue of Mutation Case No.702/1988-89 and all the relevant papers have been produced from the side of the pre-emptee-respondent during trial of the original case and after proof under the purview of Evidence Act, those papers have been marked as exhibits. He also contended that the trial Court during disposal of the original case on merit rightly after proper assessment of evidence and appreciation of law in its true perspective arrived at a conclusive decision that the pre-emptors ceased to be the co-sharers in the case land. 

 12. In this respect, pre-emptor No.2, Yusuf Chowdhury while deposing as PW1 stated during his cross-examination that he has purchased his portion of land from Shyamol Paul in the year 1986 and 1988 and constructed his dwelling house and he has separated the jama vide Mutation Case No.563 of 1988-89 and a separate Khatian being No.1686 has been created in his name on splitting the holding. He further deposed that petitioner No.1, Kabir Ahmed Chowdhury purchased 03(three) acres land from Sheuly Chakraborty who purchased the same from Shadan Dhastidhar and that he could not say as to whether Sheuly Chakraborty mutated her name and thereby separated her portion of land vide Mutation Case No. 441 of 1988-89 and that his father, Kabir Ahmed Chowdhury, also separated his portion of land vide Mutation Case No.92 of 1993-94 and thereby created a separated Khatian being No.1664. Thereafter, he deposed that he could not say as to whether there was a separate Khatian being No.1687 in the name of Bhupesh Dutto which has been created vide Mutation Case No.702 of 1988-89. 

 13. Mr. Probir Neogi, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent No.1 argued that the petitioners (pre-emptor) are no more a co-sharer in the suit khatian inasmuch as pursuant to their purchase, they got their name mutated in respect of suit land vide aforementioned mutation case and thereby they ceased to be co-sharer in respect of suit land since with the separation of holding from the joint holding and other co-sharer also being ceased to be co-sharer. On the other hand, A.M. Amin Uddin, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the petitioners (preemptor) denied the aforesaid argument and counter argued that it is to be as took into as to whether the notice of separation of holding was proceeding having been served on the co-sharer and mutation being effected behind their back and knowledge, there is no valid splitting up of jama and as such, the co-sharers have not lost their right of pre-emption under section 24 of Non Agricultural Tenancy Act. He further argued that the mutated khatian does not mean that there is the division of holding and by mutation khatian co-sharership does not extinguish the co-sharership and that in a proceeding under section 24 of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, the petitioners ought to be co-sharer of the land transferred, not in the jama. He also argued that the ingredients of pre-emption under of section 24 of the Non-Agriculture Tenancy Act and those of section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are different. The expression "holding" in section 96 is not to be found in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, He finally argued that the sub-division of holding without demarcation on the ground and not shown on the cadastral survey map is not a valid subdivision and the pre-emptee-opposite party failed to prove that after splitting jama, the land was demarcated on the ground by tri-angular pillars and that land was shown on the cadastral survey map.
